You are an adversarial verifier for a RISC-V bare-metal OS lab at /workspace.

A reviewer claims this is a bug:
  file: Project5-Device_Driver/drivers/net.c:80
  title: do_net_recv interrupt mode resumes work after scheduler(), which never happens in this kernel
  detail: In the `net_poll_mode == 1` branch the code does `do_block(...)` (line 78), `scheduler()` (line 80), and then expects execution to continue *after the RX interrupt has staged the frames* so it can copy them out (lines 83-92).

This kernel has no in-kernel continuation. `scheduler()` (kernel/sched/sched.c) only rewrites `current_running`/`current_cpu_running` and `satp`; the kernel-stack switch happens exclusively in `RESTORE_CONTEXT` inside `ret_from_exception` (arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:55, :155). A blocked task therefore resumes in *user* mode at its saved `sepc`, not at the instruction after `scheduler()`. The author's own `do_waitpid` comment in the same commit states this explicitly ("A blocked process can only be resumed in user mode, so waitpid cannot simply continue where it left off"), and every pre-existing blocking primitive follows the rule (`binsem_op` kernel/locking/binsem.c:39-41, `futex_wait` kernel/locking/futex.c:55-57 both end at `scheduler()`).

So lines 83-92 run immediately, in the same syscall invocation, before XEmacPsRecvHandler has written anything.
  why it is wrong: Two independent failures. (1) `recv_stage_len[]` is still all zeros, so `rx_tail` is 0: `sys_net_recv` returns 0 and copies nothing into the user buffer, and `recv.c` (test/recv.c:29-41) prints "0" and no packet bytes even though the frame does arrive later. (2) Far worse: `scheduler()` has already installed the *next* task's page table via `set_satp`, so `memcpy((uint8_t*)rx_curr, ...)` and `*(frLength + i) = ...` dereference the caller's user virtual addresses (`recv_buffer`, `recv_length`) in a foreign address space. Since the caller was just moved to `net_recv_queue`, `next` is frequently `kernel_pcb[cpu_id]`, whose pgdir is the boot table `PGDIR_PA` with no user mappings at all -> store page fault taken from S-mode -> `exception_handler_entry` calls the non-recursive `lock_kernel()` (kernel/sched/smp.c:30) which this hart already holds -> hard hang of the whole system. If the next task happens to have those VAs mapped, it silently corrupts that unrelated process's memory instead.

Your job is to REFUTE it. Read the actual code at that location and all surrounding context, headers, and callers. Common reasons a claim is bogus: the behavior is handled elsewhere, the lab's simplified contract does not require it, the code path is unreachable in this lab's tests, the reviewer misread a macro or pointer type, or the "fix" would break something else.

Set refuted=true unless you can positively confirm, by reading the code, that this is a genuine defect that would produce wrong runtime behavior. Default to refuted=true when uncertain.

#!/bin/bash
# Host-side functional tests for the kernel subsystems implemented in this repo.
#
# Kernel code is compiled natively (with small shims under hostshim/ standing in
# for the RISC-V specific headers) and driven directly, so the scheduling,
# synchronisation, IPC and file-system logic can be executed and asserted on
# without a board or an emulator.
set -u

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
ROOT=$(pwd)
SHIM="$ROOT/agent_tests/hostshim"
OUT=$(mktemp -d)
fail=0

run_case() {
    local name=$1; shift
    if ! gcc -g -O0 -o "$OUT/$name" "$@" 2>"$OUT/$name.log"; then
        echo "[$name] COMPILE FAILED"
        sed -n '1,40p' "$OUT/$name.log"
        fail=1
        return
    fi
    if ! timeout 60 "$OUT/$name"; then
        echo "[$name] RUN FAILED"
        fail=1
    fi
}

P2A="$ROOT/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part1"
run_case p2a_sched \
    "$ROOT/agent_tests/p2a_sched_test.c" \
    "$P2A/kernel/sched/sched.c" "$P2A/kernel/locking/lock.c" \
    -I"$SHIM" -I"$P2A/include" -I"$P2A/drivers" -I"$P2A/arch/riscv/include"

# get_ticks() reads the RISC-V `time` CSR, which the host cannot execute.  Swap
# just that one read for a counter the test drives; timer_check() -- the code
# actually under test -- is compiled verbatim.
host_time_c() {
    python3 - "$1" "$2" <<'PY'
import sys
src = open(sys.argv[1]).read()
asm = '''    __asm__ __volatile__(
        "rdtime %0"
        : "=r"(time_elapsed));'''
assert asm in src, "get_ticks() no longer looks the way the test expects"
src = src.replace(asm, "    time_elapsed = host_get_ticks();")
src = "extern unsigned long host_get_ticks(void);\n" + src
open(sys.argv[2], "w").write(src)
PY
}

P2B="$ROOT/Project2-A_Simple_Kernel_Part2"
if [ -f "$ROOT/agent_tests/p2b_sched_test.c" ]; then
    host_time_c "$P2B/kernel/sched/time.c" "$OUT/p2b_time.c"
    run_case p2b_sched \
        "$ROOT/agent_tests/p2b_sched_test.c" \
        "$P2B/kernel/sched/sched.c" "$P2B/kernel/locking/lock.c" \
        "$P2B/kernel/locking/futex.c" "$P2B/kernel/locking/binsem.c" \
        "$OUT/p2b_time.c" \

#!/bin/bash
# Build a project subtree in a scratch directory so the repo stays clean.
#
# The checked-in host tools (elf2char/createimage/generateMapping) are mode
# 644 in git and the Makefile hard-codes a cross prefix that does not exist in
# this container, so we copy the tree out and fix both there.  gcc >= 10 also
# defaults to -fno-common, which trips over the generated user_programs.h; the
# original lab toolchain was older, hence -fcommon.
#
# usage: agent_tests/build.sh <ProjectDir> [make target...]
set -u

PROJ="$1"; shift
SRC="/workspace/$PROJ"
DST="/tmp/b/$(echo "$PROJ" | cut -c1-8)"

[ -d "$SRC" ] || { echo "no such project: $SRC"; exit 2; }

rm -rf "$DST"
mkdir -p /tmp/b
cp -a "$SRC" "$DST" || exit 2
chmod +x "$DST"/elf2char "$DST"/createimage "$DST"/generateMapping 2>/dev/null

sed -i 's/^CROSS_PREFIX = .*/CROSS_PREFIX = riscv64-linux-gnu-/' "$DST/Makefile"
sed -i 's/^\(CFLAGS = .*\)$/\1 -fcommon/' "$DST/Makefile"
sed -i 's/^\(USER_CFLAGS = .*\)$/\1 -fcommon/' "$DST/Makefile"

cd "$DST" || exit 2
timeout 1200 make "${@:-main}" 2>&1

I read the code and could not refute the claim — it holds up on every point I tried to break.

**What I verified (all paths absolute):**

- `/workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/sched/sched.c:53-103` — `scheduler()` does no kernel-stack switch. It updates `current_running[cpu_id]`, `current_cpu_running`, per-task cursor, then `set_satp(SATP_MODE_SV39, 0, next->pgdir >> ...)` + `local_flush_tlb_all()`. `grep -rn "switch_to"` over the whole Project5 tree returns nothing.
- `/workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/arch/riscv/kernel/entry.S:160-162` — the stack switch is exclusively `ret_from_exception`: `ld tp, current_cpu_running` → `RESTORE_CONTEXT` → `ld sp, PCB_KERNEL_SP(tp)`. So code after `scheduler()` runs immediately, on the caller's kernel stack, with the *next* task's satp already installed.
- Every other blocking primitive obeys this: `do_sleep` (sched.c:331-336) ends at `scheduler()`; `do_waitpid` (sched.c:416-418) rewinds `regs->sepc = regs->sepc - 4` to re-execute the syscall on resume; `do_exit` only calls `enable_preempt()` afterwards, which touches `tp`/CSRs, never user memory. `do_net_send` (net.c:119-130) is likewise fine — only `enable_preempt()` follows its `scheduler()`. `do_net_recv` is the only site that does real work afterwards.
- Failure 1 confirmed: `recv_stage_len[]` (net.c:34, file-static) is still zero at net.c:86-91 — `disable_preempt()` (net.c:46) did `csrw sie, zero`, so `XEmacPsRecvHandler` (`drivers/emacps/xemacps_main.c:915-948`, the only writer of `_frLength`/`recv_stage_len`) cannot have run. `rx_tail` stays 0, and `/workspace/Project5-Device_Driver/kernel/syscall/syscall.c:9` writes that 0 into the *caller's* saved `a0`, so `test/recv.c:30` prints `0`.
